chapters.title: Acts 15 — The Jerusalem council and the welcome of Gentile believers
chapters.historicalContext: Believers from Judea argue that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. The apostles and elders gather in Jerusalem; Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and James speak, and the council sends a letter asking Gentile believers to avoid idolatry, sexual immorality, and practices that would fracture fellowship.
chapters.overview: The council addresses how Gentiles can belong to the people of God without first becoming Jews. The decision recognises the Spirit’s work and seeks a faithful, workable path for a diverse community.
chapters.studyObservation: The discussion is an internal debate among Jewish followers of Jesus. James interprets the Gentile mission through the prophets, and the letter is delivered by trusted representatives to communities beyond Jerusalem.
chapters.connectionNotes: Hold together conviction, Scripture, listening, and communal discernment. Welcome people without demanding that they erase their cultural identity, and avoid placing unnecessary burdens on those coming to faith.
chapters.lifeApplication: The council’s specific instructions arise from its first-century setting and should not be used to rank ethnic groups or control people’s bodies. The text records a negotiated decision, not contempt for Jewish practice.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Read the debate as a turning point in the church’s understanding of Gentile inclusion. Notice how testimony, Scripture, and the Spirit’s work inform the council’s decision.
keyPassages: What question brings the leaders together in Jerusalem?
How do Peter and James interpret the Spirit’s work among Gentiles?
Why does the council send a letter with trusted representatives?

chapters.title: Acts 16 — The mission enters Macedonia: Lydia, the jailer, and a new community
chapters.historicalContext: Paul and his companions travel through Asia Minor and receive a vision directing them toward Macedonia. In Philippi, Lydia welcomes the message and offers hospitality; Paul and Silas are imprisoned after freeing an enslaved girl from exploitation, and an earthquake opens the prison doors.
chapters.overview: The Gospel crosses into a new region through guidance, hospitality, confrontation with exploitation, and unexpected deliverance. The chapter ends with the jailer and his household responding and the missionaries asserting their rights as Roman citizens.
chapters.studyObservation: Lydia is a businesswoman and host whose agency helps establish the community. The enslaved girl’s exploitation is central to the conflict; the narrative should not make her suffering a mere instrument for the missionaries’ story.
chapters.connectionNotes: Practise hospitality, recognise the dignity of people exploited for profit, and respond to injustice without turning others into tools for ministry. Care for people in crisis and seek accountable use of public authority.
chapters.lifeApplication: The girl’s deliverance does not erase the injustice of slavery or guarantee that every prisoner will be freed. Paul and Silas’s decision to remain and address the officials should not be used to shame people who choose another safe response.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Trace how the mission moves from a vision to a riverside gathering, a household, and a prison. Notice the different forms of courage shown by Lydia, the enslaved girl, and the jailer.
keyPassages: How does Lydia help the new community take root in Philippi?
What injustice lies behind the accusation against Paul and Silas?
How do the missionaries respond to the jailer and to the magistrates?

chapters.title: Acts 17 — Paul in Thessalonica, Berea, and Athens
chapters.historicalContext: Paul proclaims Jesus in Thessalonica and faces opposition. In Berea, listeners examine the Scriptures carefully. In Athens, Paul speaks at the Areopagus, engaging local religious ideas and pointing to the Creator, human dependence on God, repentance, and resurrection.
chapters.overview: The chapter presents several forms of public witness: scriptural reasoning, careful examination, and engagement with a philosophical audience. Responses vary, and the message is adapted without abandoning its central claim.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul’s speech in Athens draws on language familiar to his listeners while challenging idolatry. The Bereans are praised for examining claims rather than accepting them uncritically.
chapters.connectionNotes: Study carefully, listen to the questions people actually ask, and communicate faith with clarity and respect. Let examination strengthen conviction rather than treating honest inquiry as disloyalty.
chapters.lifeApplication: Do not caricature Greek culture or portray every listener as hostile. Paul’s engagement is contextual and does not authorise manipulation or contempt for other traditions.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Compare the synagogue discussions with the Areopagus speech. Notice how Paul begins from the audience’s context and moves toward the resurrection.
keyPassages: What distinguishes the Bereans’ response to Paul’s teaching?
How does Paul connect with his Athenian audience?
Why is the resurrection a decisive point in the Areopagus speech?

chapters.title: Acts 18 — Corinth, Priscilla and Aquila, and the strengthening of the mission
chapters.historicalContext: Paul arrives in Corinth and works with Priscilla and Aquila, fellow tentmakers. He teaches in the synagogue and later remains in the city after receiving encouragement in a vision. Apollos, an eloquent teacher, is instructed more fully by Priscilla and Aquila.
chapters.overview: The chapter highlights sustained ministry, shared work, hospitality, and collaborative teaching. The mission grows through relationships and the willingness to strengthen one another’s understanding.
chapters.studyObservation: Priscilla is named alongside Aquila and plays an active role in explaining the way of God to Apollos. Gallio’s ruling provides a glimpse of the legal and political environment in which the mission operates.
chapters.connectionNotes: Value collaborative ministry, learn from others, and make room for women and men to teach and serve. Persevere with wisdom and seek encouragement when work becomes difficult.
chapters.lifeApplication: Do not reduce Priscilla to a supporting figure or claim the passage establishes one exclusive model of church leadership. Gallio’s decision is a local legal episode, not a blanket guarantee of protection.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Follow the movement from Paul’s work in Corinth to Apollos’s arrival in Ephesus. Notice how the mission is sustained by shared labour and teaching.
keyPassages: How do work and hospitality support Paul’s ministry in Corinth?
What encouragement does Paul receive during his time there?
How do Priscilla and Aquila help Apollos grow in understanding?

chapters.title: Acts 19 — The Gospel in Ephesus and the challenge to the trade in idols
chapters.historicalContext: Paul teaches in Ephesus, and extraordinary events accompany the spread of the message. Some practitioners abandon magical practices, while a silversmith named Demetrius stirs opposition because the growing movement threatens the trade in silver shrines of Artemis.
chapters.overview: The chapter shows the Gospel challenging spiritual exploitation and economic interests. Public response is mixed, and the disturbance reveals how religious identity, livelihood, and civic pride can become entangled.
chapters.studyObservation: Ephesus was a major centre of Artemis worship and commerce. The burning of expensive scrolls is presented as a costly break with former practices, while the riot is driven partly by economic anxiety.
chapters.connectionNotes: Examine practices that exploit fear or sell spiritual power. Let changed convictions reshape harmful habits, while respecting people and avoiding mob pressure or public humiliation.
chapters.lifeApplication: The account does not justify hostility toward people who worship differently. The riot is not a model for protest, and the value of discarded scrolls should not be used to demand reckless financial sacrifice.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Notice how personal transformation affects public life and how economic interests react when a profitable system is challenged.
keyPassages: What changes when the disciples receive fuller teaching about the Spirit?
Why do some people abandon magical practices?
How do economic interests shape the disturbance in Ephesus?

chapters.title: Acts 20 — Paul’s farewell to the Ephesian elders and the journey toward Jerusalem
chapters.historicalContext: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, raises Eutychus after the young man falls from a window during a long meeting, and meets the Ephesian elders at Miletus. He recalls his ministry, warns of future dangers, and entrusts the leaders to God and the word of grace.
chapters.overview: The chapter combines pastoral memory, communal worship, warning, and farewell. Paul’s journey toward Jerusalem is marked by resolve and by the grief of communities who may not see him again.
chapters.studyObservation: The speech to the elders is shaped as a farewell address, emphasising humility, service, teaching, and care for vulnerable members. Paul warns against leaders who exploit the community.
chapters.connectionNotes: Lead through service, protect those who are vulnerable, and invest in others who can continue the work. Receive grief honestly when seasons of ministry or relationship change.
chapters.lifeApplication: Paul’s warnings must not become a tool for leaders to silence questions or declare themselves beyond accountability. The account does not require people to ignore safety or accept abusive leadership.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Read the farewell speech slowly and identify the qualities Paul commends. Notice how care for the community is more important than personal status.
keyPassages: What does the story of Eutychus reveal about the gathered community?
Which qualities does Paul recall from his ministry among the elders?
What warning does Paul give about future leadership?

chapters.title: Acts 21 — Paul returns to Jerusalem and faces a public accusation
chapters.historicalContext: Paul travels toward Jerusalem despite warnings about danger. He meets believers along the way, visits James and the elders, participates in a purification rite, and is accused by a crowd in the temple. Roman soldiers intervene and take him into custody.
chapters.overview: The chapter shows Paul trying to maintain fellowship across Jewish and Gentile believers while navigating suspicion and public hostility. His arrest begins a new phase in which he will testify under Roman custody.
chapters.studyObservation: The purification rite reflects Paul’s Jewish identity and his willingness to respect communal concerns. The accusation about the temple is based on a misunderstanding involving Trophimus, a Gentile believer.
chapters.connectionNotes: Do not assume that faithfulness always avoids conflict. Seek peace across differences, correct misinformation, and protect people from mob violence and false accusation.
chapters.lifeApplication: The scene must not be used to portray Jewish people collectively as violent or hostile. The crowd is a specific group in a charged situation, and Roman intervention is an exercise of imperial power.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Follow Paul’s route and the repeated warnings he receives. Notice his effort to maintain unity and the way rumours escalate into violence.
keyPassages: Why does Paul agree to participate in the purification rite?
What accusation triggers the crowd’s violence?
How does the Roman commander’s intervention change Paul’s situation?

chapters.title: Acts 22 — Paul’s testimony to the Jerusalem crowd
chapters.historicalContext: Paul addresses the crowd in Aramaic and recounts his Jewish upbringing, persecution of the Jesus movement, encounter with Jesus on the road to Damascus, and commission to witness. The crowd reacts strongly, and Paul invokes his Roman citizenship when officials prepare to flog him.
chapters.overview: Paul’s testimony connects his former life with his calling and demonstrates how personal witness can be offered within a tense public setting. His legal status becomes important in preventing unlawful punishment.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul speaks as a Jew trained in Jerusalem and identifies with the audience’s language and history. His testimony includes Ananias and the vision in the temple, while the crowd’s reaction reflects conflict over his mission to Gentiles.
chapters.connectionNotes: Tell the truth about transformation without erasing the past. Use lawful protections where available and do not mistake suffering for proof that a person has done wrong.
chapters.lifeApplication: The crowd’s reaction must not be generalised to all Jewish people. Paul’s Roman citizenship is a legal protection, not a reason to shame those without such status.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Notice how Paul establishes common ground before describing the turning point in his life. Consider why the Gentile mission becomes the flashpoint.
keyPassages: How does Paul build a connection with the crowd?
What role does Ananias play in Paul’s testimony?
How does Roman citizenship protect Paul from unlawful flogging?

chapters.title: Acts 23 — Paul before the council and the plot against his life
chapters.historicalContext: Paul appears before the Jewish council, where a dispute between Pharisees and Sadducees erupts. The Roman commander removes him for safety, and Paul receives encouragement that he will testify in Rome. A group plots to kill him, but his nephew warns the authorities and the plot is stopped.
chapters.overview: The chapter shows the complexity of legal and religious conflict under Roman rule. Paul’s safety depends on intervention, careful procedure, and the courage of a family member who reports a threat.
chapters.studyObservation: The council includes differing Jewish movements with distinct beliefs about resurrection and angels. The narrative describes a specific political and legal conflict, not a judgement on Judaism as a whole.
chapters.connectionNotes: Seek truthful process, protect people threatened with violence, and recognise that courage may come from unexpected people. Do not exploit divisions to inflame conflict.
chapters.lifeApplication: Paul’s appeal to resurrection is not permission to manipulate religious disagreements. The plot is criminal violence and must not be romanticised as religious zeal.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Read the council scene with attention to the different positions represented. Then follow the practical steps that prevent the planned ambush.
keyPassages: What causes the disagreement between Pharisees and Sadducees?
How does Paul receive encouragement in the midst of danger?
What role does Paul’s nephew play in preventing the plot?

chapters.title: Acts 24 — Paul’s hearing before Felix
chapters.historicalContext: Paul is brought to Caesarea and accused before the governor Felix. He answers the charges, explains his hope in the resurrection, and speaks about righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment. Felix delays a decision and keeps Paul in custody while hoping for a bribe.
chapters.overview: The chapter contrasts a clear defence with a governor who delays justice for political and personal reasons. Paul’s faith remains focused on conscience and resurrection while the legal process stalls.
chapters.studyObservation: The accusations concern public disorder, the movement called the Way, and the temple. Felix’s handling of the case illustrates the vulnerabilities of provincial justice under Roman administration.
chapters.connectionNotes: Maintain integrity when decisions are delayed, speak truthfully under accusation, and refuse bribery. Remember people whose freedom is limited by unjust or self-serving systems.
chapters.lifeApplication: Paul’s imprisonment should not be treated as evidence of guilt or as a spiritual ideal. The text criticises delay and corruption rather than presenting the governor’s conduct as acceptable.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Compare the accusers’ claims with Paul’s response. Notice how Felix’s private conversations differ from the public question of justice.
keyPassages: How does Paul answer the accusations brought by Tertullus?
What does Paul say about his hope and conscience?
How does Felix’s desire for money affect the case?

chapters.title: Acts 25 — Paul appeals to Caesar before Festus and King Agrippa
chapters.historicalContext: Festus succeeds Felix and hears renewed accusations against Paul. When pressure grows to move the case to Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar. Festus consults King Agrippa, whose visit provides an opportunity to explain the case and the dispute surrounding Jesus’ resurrection.
chapters.overview: The chapter moves Paul’s testimony toward Rome through a formal appeal. Political calculations and legal procedure shape the path, while the central issue remains the proclamation of Jesus alive.
chapters.studyObservation: The appeal to Caesar is a legal right within the Roman system. Festus’ consultation with Agrippa reflects the complexity of provincial administration and the need to clarify charges before sending a prisoner onward.
chapters.connectionNotes: Use lawful processes wisely, distinguish evidence from political pressure, and keep truth central when powerful people discuss a person’s fate.
chapters.lifeApplication: The chapter does not celebrate empire or imply that Roman justice is always fair. Paul’s appeal is a response to a particular danger and legal situation.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Track how Festus handles the case and why Paul refuses a transfer that could expose him to danger. Notice how the issue is framed for Agrippa.
keyPassages: Why does Paul appeal to Caesar?
What political pressures influence Festus’ decision?
What problem does Festus need Agrippa to help clarify?

chapters.title: Acts 26 — Paul’s defence before Agrippa and the call to turn toward the light
chapters.historicalContext: Paul recounts his life as a Pharisee, his persecution of believers, and his encounter with the risen Jesus. He explains his mission to Jews and Gentiles, calling people to repentance and changed lives. Festus calls him mad, while Agrippa questions whether Paul can persuade him.
chapters.overview: The chapter is a carefully shaped testimony that links Paul’s calling with Israel’s hope and the resurrection. Paul presents his mission as obedience to a heavenly vision rather than a pursuit of personal power.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul grounds his message in the Law and Prophets and emphasises continuity with Israel’s hope. The hearing is both a legal defence and a public explanation of the Gospel before rulers.
chapters.connectionNotes: Speak with clarity and respect even before powerful audiences. Let changed conduct accompany testimony, and do not measure faithfulness by whether every listener agrees.
chapters.lifeApplication: Paul’s appeal to repentance must not be used to coerce or humiliate. The narrative does not authorise contempt toward those who remain unconvinced.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Follow the repeated account of Paul’s encounter with Jesus and note what he says his mission requires. Compare the responses of Festus and Agrippa.
keyPassages: How does Paul connect his testimony with Israel’s hope?
What does Paul say his encounter with Jesus commissioned him to do?
How do Festus and Agrippa respond differently to Paul’s defence?

chapters.title: Acts 27 — The voyage to Rome and the shipwreck
chapters.historicalContext: Paul sails toward Rome under guard. Despite his warning about the danger of continuing, the ship is caught in a violent storm. Paul encourages the crew and passengers, assures them that lives will be spared, and the ship finally runs aground near Malta.
chapters.overview: The chapter portrays courage, practical leadership, and shared survival in a crisis. Paul’s confidence in God does not prevent the storm, but it strengthens him to encourage others and act wisely.
chapters.studyObservation: The voyage reflects ancient Mediterranean sailing conditions and the risks of seasonal travel. The narrative gives attention to the crew’s expertise, the soldiers’ decisions, and the practical steps taken to survive.
chapters.connectionNotes: In crisis, combine hope with practical action, listen to sound advice, and protect everyone’s life. Encourage others without denying danger or promising outcomes beyond what can be known.
chapters.lifeApplication: Paul’s warning and the eventual survival are a particular narrative event, not a formula that guarantees rescue in every disaster. Do not use the story to blame victims of shipwrecks or other tragedies.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Trace the decisions made as the storm intensifies. Notice how Paul’s calm leadership grows through encouragement, shared food, and concrete safety measures.
keyPassages: Why does Paul warn against continuing the voyage?
How does Paul encourage the people during the storm?
What practical actions help everyone survive the shipwreck?

chapters.title: Acts 28 — Malta, Paul’s arrival in Rome, and the open-ended witness
chapters.historicalContext: On Malta, Paul survives a snakebite and participates in the healing of the island’s sick. After three months he travels to Rome, where he lives under guard and welcomes visitors, explaining the kingdom of God and teaching about Jesus. Acts ends with his witness continuing openly.
chapters.overview: The final chapter brings the journey to Rome but leaves the mission open. The word continues to be proclaimed despite restrictions, and the narrative closes without describing Paul’s later fate.
chapters.studyObservation: The islanders’ response to Paul changes from suspicion to honour, while the snakebite story is not presented as a technique for proving spiritual status. The ending echoes the book’s theme of the word spreading despite opposition.
chapters.connectionNotes: Offer practical care wherever you are, welcome conversation, and continue faithful witness within real limitations. Let the open ending invite readers to consider their own part in the continuing story.
chapters.lifeApplication: Do not treat the snakebite account as permission to test God or reject medical care. The final verses do not tell us exactly what happened to Paul afterward, so avoid presenting speculation as fact.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Notice how the journey’s final stages combine hospitality, healing, and teaching. The open ending asks how the message will continue beyond the pages of Acts.
keyPassages: How do the people of Malta respond to Paul and his companions?
What does Paul’s life under guard in Rome reveal about the mission?
Why might Acts end with the message still being proclaimed?
